title: The teacher and lineage
hook: a Tibetan teacher reads a text aloud to students who could read it themselves, and that's the point

segments.voice: Yesterday, om mani padme hum, spun in wheels and carved in stone. Your line was the jewel in the lotus. Did you find the chant and listen all the way through? Today, how a practice like that gets handed on. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-seven.

A room full of students, each with a copy of the text in front of them. Every one of them can read. And yet a teacher at the front reads the whole thing aloud, quickly, sometimes so fast it's hard to follow, from the first line to the last. Nobody's taking notes. Nobody's asking questions. It can look, from the back of the room, like a strange use of an afternoon. But in Tibetan Buddhism, something is being handed over that isn't on the page: permission, connection, a living link back through the people who read it to the people who read it to this teacher. Today's word is that chain of people.
screen: `EVERYONE HAS THE TEXT.` → `THE TEACHER READS IT ALOUD.` → `SOMETHING NOT ON THE PAGE.`

segments.voice: Back on day one thousand three hundred fifty-seven, Zen showed us the teacher face to face. Tibetan Buddhism puts the teacher at the center too, with its own shape. Four turns. First, the teacher. In Tibetan the word is lama, used for the Sanskrit guru. Tibetan texts treat the teacher as the doorway to practice, the one who makes the teaching alive for a particular student. Second, the reading. What happened in that room is called a lung, a reading transmission. The text is read aloud so it's received by ear from someone who received it the same way. Third, empowerment. Some Tibetan practices, especially the ones involving visualizing a buddha or reciting certain mantras, are begun only after an empowerment, a ceremony in which a qualified teacher introduces the student to that practice. Some texts and practices are meant to stay closed until then. Not because they're secret for the sake of it, the tradition says, but because done without guidance they can be misunderstood. Fourth, the lineage. Each practice is said to come down an unbroken chain, teacher to student, and lineages have prayers that name the chain one person at a time. Practicing means stepping into that line. Here's the balance the tradition itself keeps: Tibetan texts on finding a teacher warn the student to examine a teacher carefully, sometimes for a long time, before trusting them. Respect for the teacher and care in choosing one belong together. The idea underneath is simple enough to hold on an ordinary Tuesday. Some things can be learned from a book. Some can't.
screen: `THE LAMA, THE DOORWAY.` · `THE READING: RECEIVED BY EAR.` · `EMPOWERMENT BEFORE PRACTICE.` · `A CHAIN OF PEOPLE, AND CARE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respect what needs a teacher. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind something you've been trying to learn alone, from books or videos. An instrument. A language. A practice of prayer or meditation. Where does it keep stalling? Then ask the question the Tibetan texts ask: if a guide were to help with this, what would you want to see in them before trusting them? Patience? Honesty? Their own practice? Don't decide anything. Just let the question sit. The bell holds the time.
The teacher and lineage. In Tibetan Buddhism, the lama who gives the reading and the empowerment, and the chain of teachers behind them. Today's word.
Your line: some things need a teacher. Today, ask one question about the thing you've been learning alone, of someone who knows it better than you. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism, students receive a practice from a teacher through a reading transmission, an empowerment and instructions, and lineages recite prayers naming the teachers who passed it down.

original.note: Tibetan bla ma: teacher, used for the Sanskrit guru.

trapdoor: what you thought: a lama is a Tibetan monk.
what it means: a lama is a teacher who passes a practice on by reading, empowerment and instruction.
what a scholar hears: lung, wang and lineage prayers: the teaching travels person to person, and the texts also urge testing the teacher first.

sources.ref: Tibetan Buddhist practice of reading transmission (lung) and empowerment (wang)

notes: Different angle from day 1357 (Zen, face to face): this day centers lung, empowerment and lineage prayers; 1357 is referenced once.
Lama is used for Sanskrit guru; not every monk is a lama, which the trapdoor floor 1 plays on; confirm the framing.
'Sometimes for a long time' about examining a teacher softens popular 'twelve years' claims; confirm the Lamrim Chenmo citation for the teacher's qualities.
Restricted practices described as closed until empowerment 'because done without guidance they can be misunderstood': confirm this is a fair summary of the tradition's reason.
The hook's fast reading aloud is a common feature of lung; confirm.
